exam: A 28‑year‑old man with chronic cough and bilateral clubbing – what is the most likely diagnosis and why? — Look for chronic hypoxic lung disease; TB or bronchiectasis are common in East Africa.
You see clubbing in a 5‑year‑old with a heart murmur – what is your next investigation? — Perform an ECG and refer for echocardiography to assess cyanotic congenital heart disease.

A patient with clubbing presents with fever and haemoptysis – what is your immediate management step? — Obtain sputum for AFB and start empiric anti‑TB therapy if high suspicion, while arranging infection control.

Explain the pathophysiological basis of clubbing and how it guides your differential diagnosis. — Vascular proliferation driven by growth factors links clubbing to chronic hypoxia or inflammation, narrowing differentials to pulmonary, cardiac, or systemic disease.
When is it appropriate to order a CT chest in a low‑resource setting for clubbing? — If chest X‑ray is normal but suspicion for bronchiectasis or early malignancy remains high and CT is available.
Why would high‑dose oral steroids be avoided in most patients with clubbing? — Steroids do not treat the underlying hypoxic or infectious cause and increase infection risk.
Differentiate clubbing from pachydermoperiostosis on exam. — Clubbing lacks painful joint swelling and skin thickening; pachydermoperiostosis has periostitis and skin changes.
What red‑flag symptom in a clubbing patient mandates urgent referral? — New onset chest pain or haemoptysis suggests possible lung cancer or severe infection.
ai.title: Digital Clubbing
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Clubbing is a bulbous enlargement of the distal phalanges caused by chronic hypoxia or vascular inflammation. Recognise it at the bedside, link it to underlying disease, and know the limited investigations available in low‑resource settings.

b: Often painless and bilateral
Develops over weeks to months
Associated with chronic hypoxia, inflammation, or neoplasia
sections.p: Clubbing is a permanent, symmetrical swelling of the nail bed and distal finger, giving a convex nail plate and loss of the normal angle between nail and skin.

b: Clubbing = increased nail‑bed angle (Lovibond angle >160°)
Schamroth window test: absent diamond‑shaped gap when fingertips are opposed
sections.p: The pathophysiology involves increased blood flow, vasodilation, and connective‑tissue proliferation driven by platelet‑derived growth factor and vascular endothelial growth factor.

b: Prioritise evaluation for chronic respiratory disease (TB, bronchiectasis, COPD)
Consider congenital cyanotic heart disease in children
Look for gastrointestinal or hepatic disease (cirrhosis, inflammatory bowel disease)
Rarely, paraneoplastic lung cancer
sections.p: Clubbing is a visual clue to serious underlying disease; in low‑resource hospitals it often points to chronic lung disease, congenital heart disease, or infection.

t.b: Identify chronic lung pathology, cavitation, or masses; a normal film does not exclude early disease
Detect chronic hypoxia; <92% suggests need for further respiratory work‑up
Screen for right‑heart strain or congenital lesions when cardiac cause suspected
Look for polycythaemia (chronic hypoxia) or eosinophilia (parasitic infection); if unavailable, rely on clinical picture
Rule out pulmonary TB, a common cause of chronic hypoxia in East Africa

b: For chronic lung disease: bronchodilators, inhaled steroids, pulmonary rehabilitation; avoid high‑dose oral steroids unless indicated
TB: standard 6‑month regimen (rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol); monitor liver function
Cyanotic heart disease: refer for surgical correction when feasible; give prophylactic antibiotics for endocarditis risk
Supportive: smoking cessation, nutrition optimisation, oxygen therapy if SpO2 <90%
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause; supportive measures improve quality of life while specific therapy addresses the disease.

b: Pachydermoperiostosis – hereditary, painful joint swelling, no underlying disease
Acromegaly – enlarged hands with coarse facial features, GH excess
Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy secondary to lung cancer – similar signs but often unilateral and painful

Polycythaemia may be absent in early hypoxia; rely on clinical trend

Correlate clubbing with respiratory symptoms, cyanosis, or cardiac murmur
